title: Short Stuff: Liquid Paper
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Betty Claire McMurray (later Betty Nesmith Graham), the Dallas typist who invented Liquid Paper (originally called "Mistake Out") as a correction fluid after carbon ribbons made typing errors harder to erase. The episode covers her early work in her kitchen, the growth of the Liquid Paper Company, her foundations supporting women and the arts, her ouster by second husband Robert Graham in a boardroom takeover, her regaining control, and the 1979 sale to Gillette for nearly $48 million. It closes with notes on the enduring correction-products market and a tribute to Mike Nesmith, her son and a member of the Monkees.

segments.title: Introduction to Betty Nesmith Graham
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as part of the women who changed history series, naming Betty Claire McMurray (Betty Nesmith Graham) as the inventor of Liquid Paper and noting her connection to Mike Nesmith of the Monkees.

segments.title: Typing job and origin of Liquid Paper
segments.summary: Betty, a young divorced single mother, worked as a typist at Texas Bank and Trust. When typewriters switched from fabric to carbon ribbons, mistakes could no longer be erased easily. She made a tempera-based correction fluid, first called Mistake Out, and co-workers began asking for it.

segments.title: Refining the product in her kitchen
segments.summary: Betty refined the formula at home with help from a paint company employee and a high school chemistry teacher. Her son Mike and his friends filled bottles for about a dollar an hour. She left or was let go from the bank after an incident involving a business document.

segments.title: Building the Liquid Paper Company
segments.summary: After leaving the bank in 1958, Betty took orders from large corporations such as GE and IBM, patented the product, renamed the business Liquid Paper Company, and grew from a kitchen to a backyard to a four-room house. She remarried Robert Graham in 1962. By 1968 the company had nineteen employees and sold one million bottles.

segments.title: Company culture and Betty's philanthropy
segments.summary: By 1975 the company had a 35,000 square foot Dallas headquarters and 500-bottle-per-minute equipment. Betty offered an on-site library and child care center. She funded the Gihan Foundation to collect art by women and founded the Betty Claire McMurray Foundation in 1978 to support women in need.

segments.title: Hostile takeover by Robert Graham and sale to Gillette
segments.summary: After her divorce from Robert Graham and her step back as chair, Graham ousted her in a boardroom takeover, changed the formula to cut off her royalties, and kept her from the premises. She eventually regained control and sold Liquid Paper to Gillette for almost $48 million. She reportedly told Robert to get out of her office.

segments.title: Modern correction products market and Mike Nesmith tribute
segments.summary: The hosts note that Liquid Paper has held its market share while office paper and printers declined, with artists and Gen Z interest helping. They pay tribute to Mike Nesmith's solo country rock work.

segments.title: Credits and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck credit sources including The Atlantic, David Graham, Thought Co, Mary Bellis, and the Gihan Foundation, and close the episode.
